title: An erosion control and soil conservation method for agrarian uses based on determining the erosion threshold
author: Blanco-Sepúlveda

steps.title: Set up visual indicator coding
steps.instruction: Apply the adapted presence/absence test of visual indicators and assign the codes shown in Tables 1‑2: primary types E (erosion), P (tool disturbance), T (trampling), D (deposition), C (compaction), N (no erosion) and O (others) with sub‑indices (Ei, Es, Er, Eg, Pes, Pi/Ps/Pr/Pg, Tes, Ti/Ts/Tr/Tg, Des, Di/Ds/Dr/Dg, Nw, Nl, Nf, Or, Oa). Note that Pes indicates soil disturbed by tools to a depth of 2–3 cm with a granular structure <1 cm, which can evolve to Ps when the granular structure disappears.

steps.title: Design sampling layout
steps.instruction: Divide each plot into four quadrants. Randomly select three quadrants by drawing numbered balls from a set of 1‑4. For each selected quadrant determine a start point (Yn, Xn) by drawing a numbered ball that gives the distance in metres along the X‑ and Y‑axes from the plot centre (point 0). Choose the sampling method based on land use: use grids for homogeneous crops (maize, beans) or transects for heterogeneous or agroforestry systems.

substeps.instruction: If using grids, prepare two sets of grids: small 0.6 × 0.6 m grids for erosion‑state assessment and larger 3 × 3 m grids for soil‑loss measurement.
If using transects, lay linear samples of at least 10 m (or diagonal 4 m from point 0 for ground‑cover transects).

steps.title: Establish observation points
steps.instruction: For each 0.6 × 0.6 m grid divide each side into six 0.1 m sections and record observations at every intersection (36 points per grid). Use three such grids per plot → 108 observations (each point = 0.9 % of total sample). For each 10 m transect mark points every 0.25 m (40 points per transect); three transects give 120 observations (each point = 0.8 % of total sample). At every point record the visual‑indicator code, ground‑cover class (bare soil, weeds, litter, stones, others) and aerial‑cover class (herbaceous, shrub, tree).

steps.title: Measure slope and aerial cover
steps.instruction: In each quadrant measure slope gradient with a manual clinometer; calculate the mean of the four measurements to represent the plot slope. Measure the height of the aerial vegetal strata with a laser distance meter.

steps.title: Collect and prepare soil sample
steps.instruction: At point 0 of each plot collect a surface soil sample from the top 10 cm. Air‑dry the sample, then pass it through a 2 mm mesh sieve and retain the fine fraction for laboratory analysis.

steps.title: Laboratory analysis of soil
steps.instruction: Analyse the sieved sample for texture (fraction distribution), organic‑matter content and calcium‑carbonate equivalent using standard laboratory methods.

steps.title: Quantify erosion state
steps.instruction: Calculate the percentage of surface area affected by erosion by dividing the number of observation points showing any erosion indicator (E, P, T, D, C) by the total number of points and expressing the result as a percent of the plot surface.

steps.title: Calculate soil‑loss volume
steps.instruction: Within each 3 × 3 m soil‑loss grid locate all rills (R) and gullies (G); measure their length, width and depth. Assume a cross‑sectional shape (semi‑elliptical, semicircular, triangular or trapezoidal) to compute the volume of each feature, sum the volumes and express the total as m³ ha⁻¹.

steps.title: Determine erodibility factors
steps.instruction: From the coded observations quantify the occurrence of activities P (ploughing/weeding), T (trampling) and C (compaction); use these frequencies as erodibility factors for the plot.

steps.title: Compute erosion threshold
steps.instruction: Combine the erosion‑state percentage, soil‑loss volume (m³ ha⁻¹), mean slope gradient and the erodibility factors (P, T, C) in the study’s defined formula to calculate the erosion threshold for the plot.

steps.title: Verify erosion threshold
steps.instruction: Compare the calculated erosion threshold with the observed field measurements (percentage affected area and measured soil‑loss volume) to confirm its validity.
